To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mutations in ABCC2 and KCNJ11 were the common causes of CHI in this large cohort.
mutations in ABCC2/KCNJ11 are the commonest genetic causes of congenital hyperinsulinaemia.
mutations in ABCC2 and ABCC8 are the commonest identifiable causes of CHI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular basis of the development of diabetes and its complications.
understanding how genetic mutations cause disease, and the role that the environment plays in the disease process.
identifying the molecular basis of CHI and the role of the genetic diagnosis on clinical management of patients with CHIs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most common genetic cause of CHI is a heterozygous mutation in the ABBC8 gene.
mutations in ABCC2/KCNJ11 are the commonest genetic causes of CHI, followed by HNF4A, GLUD1 and HADH.

mutations in ABCC2/KCNJ11 are the commonest genetic aetiology of congenital hyperinsulism, and that mutations in the ABCC2/KCJN11 genes are the commonest cause of diazoxide unresponsive congenital hyperinsuism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have characterised the largest cohort of CHI patients to date.
we have identified mutations in ABCC 8 and KCNJ 11 in 36.3% of the patients, in HADH in 1%, in GLUD1 in 5.3%, in HNF4A in 3.7%, and in GCK in 0.3%.
we have identified the commonest genetic causes of CHI and have characterised the phenotype-genotype correlations in this disorder.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of patients with congenital hypoglycaemia have an underlying genetic diagnosis, which is important for the management of patients with hypoglycaemic crises and for genetic counselling.
